# Draft:Non-daily smoking

Non-daily smoking
Non-daily smoking (also referred to as intermittent or occasional smoking) describes a pattern of cigarette use in which individuals smoke on some days but not every day. This pattern has become increasingly prevalent, particularly among young adults and certain subpopulations (Gutierrez-Torres et al., 2025; Doran et al., 2023).
Despite its growing relevance, there is no universally accepted definition of non-daily smoking. Most studies rely on self-reported frequency, such as “smoking on some days” or “less than daily,” but the specific criteria vary widely across studies (Doran et al., 2023; Nollen et al., 2020; Hoeppner et al., 2025).
Definitions and classification
Non-daily smoking is generally defined in contrast to daily smoking, but operational definitions differ across studies and surveillance systems. Common definitions include:
Smoking on fewer than 30 days in the past month
Smoking on “some days” rather than “every day”
Smoking within a specified range (e.g., 1–29 days or 4–27 days per month) (Shiffman et al., 2020; Cabriales et al., 2019)
Some definitions also incorporate lifetime cigarette thresholds (e.g., ≥100 cigarettes) or minimum frequency criteria (e.g., at least one cigarette per week) (Inoue-Choi et al., 2020; Faulkner et al., 2020).
Use in research and surveillance
Non-daily smoking is widely assessed in both clinical trials and epidemiological studies. Major surveillance systems—including NHIS, BRFSS, NHANES, PATH, and NSDUH—commonly classify individuals as non-daily smokers if they report smoking on “some days” rather than daily (VanFrank et al., 2024).
These systems often rely on simplified categorical measures, though definitions vary across datasets.
Variability in definitions
Substantial heterogeneity exists in how non-daily smoking is defined:
Some studies include individuals who have never been daily smokers, while others include former daily smokers who now smoke intermittently (Doran et al., 2023)
Frequency thresholds vary widely across studies
Cigarettes per day are inconsistently used to classify smoking intensity (Omole et al., 2020)
Most studies rely on self-report, with limited biochemical verification (Nollen et al., 2020)
This variability complicates comparisons across studies and limits standardization.

Implications for smoking cessation research
The lack of standardized definitions has several implications:
Reduced comparability of intervention outcomes across studies
Difficulty identifying effective interventions for non-daily smokers
Limited generalizability to real-world populations (Doran et al., 2023; Hoeppner et al., 2021)
Non-daily smokers represent a heterogeneous population with diverse behavioral patterns, including social and situational smoking (Omole et al., 2020).
Recommendations and future directions
Recent literature recommends:
Reporting both frequency (days smoked) and quantity (cigarettes per day)
Tracking transitions between daily and non-daily smoking
Using multiple definitions to improve comparability (Doran et al., 2023)
However, adoption of these recommendations remains inconsistent.
Conclusion
Non-daily smoking is a widely studied but inconsistently defined pattern of tobacco use. While commonly described as smoking on some days but not daily, variability in definitions limits comparability across studies and complicates research interpretation. Standardization remains an important goal for advancing tobacco research and clinical practice (Doran et al., 2023).
